claim: Unsupervised segmentation in biological and non-biological images is only partially resolved.
source: Unsupervised segmentation in biological and non-biological images is only partially resolved.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Segmentation either requires arbitrary thresholds or large teaching datasets.
source: Segmentation either requires arbitrary thresholds or large teaching datasets.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about current segmentation methods.

claim: The spatial autocorrelation method based on Local Moran's I coefficient can differentiate signal, background, and noise in any type of image.
source: Here, we propose a spatial autocorrelation method based on Local Moran's I coefficient to differentiate signal, background, and noise in any type of image.
evidence: This is the main methodological claim supported by the experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Local Moran's I method was originally described for geoinformatics.
source: The method, originally described for geoinformatics, does not require a predefined intensity threshold or teaching algorithm for image segmentation and allows quantitative comparison of samples obtained in different conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original geoinformatics literature in the introduction.

claim: Moran's method does not require a predefined intensity threshold or teaching algorithm for image segmentation.
source: The method, originally described for geoinformatics, does not require a predefined intensity threshold or teaching algorithm for image segmentation and allows quantitative comparison of samples obtained in different conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the methodological description and comparative experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Moran's method allows quantitative comparison of samples obtained in different conditions.
source: The method, originally described for geoinformatics, does not require a predefined intensity threshold or teaching algorithm for image segmentation and allows quantitative comparison of samples obtained in different conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the application to biological samples with varying noise levels.

claim: Moran's method utilizes relative intensity as well as spatial information of neighboring elements to select spatially contiguous groups of pixels.
source: It utilizes relative intensity as well as spatial information of neighboring elements to select spatially contiguous groups of pixels.
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Moran's method outperforms threshold-based method in both artificially generated as well as in natural images especially when background noise is substantial.
source: We demonstrate that Moran's method outperforms threshold-based method in both artificially generated as well as in natural images especially when background noise is substantial.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparisons shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The superior performance of Moran's method can be attributed to the exclusion of false positive pixels resulting from isolated, high intensity pixels in high noise conditions.
source: This superior performance can be attributed to the exclusion of false positive pixels resulting from isolated, high intensity pixels in high noise conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis of false positive rates in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Moran's method identified high-intensity Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 ion channel clusters in the thalamic neuropil.
source: Moran's method identified high-intensity Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 ion channel clusters in the thalamic neuropil.
evidence: This is demonstrated through confocal microscopy images and segmentation results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Spatial distribution of Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 clusters displayed strong correlation with large sensory axon terminals of subcortical origin.
source: Spatial distribution of these clusters displayed strong correlation with large sensory axon terminals of subcortical origin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through double immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The unique association of the special presynaptic terminals and a postsynaptic voltage-gated ion channel cluster was confirmed with electron microscopy.
source: The unique association of the special presynaptic terminals and a postsynaptic voltage-gated ion channel cluster was confirmed with electron microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through electron microscopy images shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Moran's method is a rapid, simple image segmentation method optimal for variable and high noise conditions.
source: These data demonstrate that Moran's method is a rapid, simple image segmentation method optimal for variable and high noise conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative performance data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pixels constituting an image can be divided into spatially non-overlapping regions which are characterized by statistically similar intrinsic features.
source: Differentiation of signal from noise is a key step in any image segmentation process (Pham et al., 2000) and is based on the assumption that pixels constituting the image can be divided into spatially non-overlapping regions which are characterized by statistically similar intrinsic features (Haralick and Shapiro, 1985; Pal and Pal, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established image segmentation literature.

claim: Signal can be defined as a spatially congruent population of pixels with gray values which are statistically different from the neighboring pixels.
source: During the segmentation process, the signal can be defined as a spatially congruent population of pixels with gray values, which are statistically different from the neighboring pixels, that is, from the background (Pham et al., 2000; Pal and Pal, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to image segmentation literature.

claim: A theoretically optimal segmentation process should be independent of the person performing the analysis.
source: A theoretically optimal segmentation process should be independent of the person performing the analysis and should be based on the intrinsic properties of the image rather than manually defined values.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle stated by the authors.

claim: An optimal segmentation process should consider not only the intensities but also the spatial arrangement of the picture elements.
source: It should consider not only the intensities but also the spatial arrangement of the picture elements (i.e., pixels).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle that motivates the use of Moran's method.

claim: Current segmentation methods are either based on hard or soft computing.
source: The current segmentation methods are either based on hard or soft computing (Sinha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of segmentation methods.

claim: There is a huge surge of soft computation methods based on fuzzy logic, deep learning methods neuronal networks and artificial intelligence.
source: Though there is huge surge of soft computation methods based on fuzzy logic, deep learning methods neuronal networks and artificial intelligence (Dey et al., 2018; Hemanth and Anitha, 2014; Devi et al., 2021), image analysis based on binary, hard computation methods have their own advantages (Jena et al., 2020) and best results can be expected from the combination of the two (Perfilieva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on computational methods.

claim: Image analysis based on binary, hard computation methods have their own advantages.
source: Though there is huge surge of soft computation methods based on fuzzy logic, deep learning methods neuronal networks and artificial intelligence (Dey et al., 2018; Hemanth and Anitha, 2014; Devi et al., 2021), image analysis based on binary, hard computation methods have their own advantages (Jena et al., 2020) and best results can be expected from the combination of the two (Perfilieva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Best results can be expected from the combination of hard and soft computing methods.
source: Though there is huge surge of soft computation methods based on fuzzy logic, deep learning methods neuronal networks and artificial intelligence (Dey et al., 2018; Hemanth and Anitha, 2014; Devi et al., 2021), image analysis based on binary, hard computation methods have their own advantages (Jena et al., 2020) and best results can be expected from the combination of the two (Perfilieva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Many hard computing image segmentation methods depend on thresholding.
source: Many hard computing image segmentation methods depend on thresholding (Sinha et al., 2020; Sahoo et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on thresholding methods.

claim: More advanced threshold-based methods utilize local not global thresholds or multilevel thresholding.
source: Although more advanced threshold-based methods (TBMs) utilize local not global thresholds or multilevel thresholding (Manikandan et al., 2014; Umaa Mageswari et al., 2013), the threshold is still defined using the intrinsic properties of the image (e.g., as deviation from the mean intensity in the picture), selection of the degree of deviation is subjective and can yield different results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Selection of the degree of deviation in threshold-based methods is subjective and can yield different results.
source: Although more advanced threshold-based methods (TBMs) utilize local not global thresholds or multilevel thresholding (Manikandan et al., 2014; Umaa Mageswari et al., 2013), the threshold is still defined using the intrinsic properties of the image (e.g., as deviation from the mean intensity in the picture), selection of the degree of deviation is subjective and can yield different results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing different results at different threshold levels.

claim: In local thresholding there is no guarantee that spatially inhomogeneous noise reaching or approaching the intensity of the signal will not be included as signal.
source: Furthermore, even in local thresholding there is no guarantee that spatially inhomogeneous noise reaching or approaching the intensity of the signal will not be included as signal.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of threshold-based methods.

claim: Local Moran's spatial correlation coefficient was originally invented for geoinformatics.
source: The method was originally invented for geoinformatics and was used to study large-scale spatial correlation of geological (Moran, 1948; Getis and Ord, 1992), social, or medical events for example suicide rates among counties (Helbich et al., 2015) or in geomorphological studies (Alvioli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original geoinformatics literature.

claim: Local Moran's method was used to study large-scale spatial correlation of geological, social, or medical events.
source: The method was originally invented for geoinformatics and was used to study large-scale spatial correlation of geological (Moran, 1948; Getis and Ord, 1992), social, or medical events for example suicide rates among counties (Helbich et al., 2015) or in geomorphological studies (Alvioli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to applications in various fields.

claim: The proposed method allows for selecting spatially congruent pixels with statistically similar intensity and pixels with intensity distribution not significantly different from random.
source: The proposed method allows for selecting spatially congruent pixels with statistically similar intensity (i.e., signal and background) and pixels with intensity distribution not significantly different from random (i.e., noise).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: At zero noise, both Moran's and threshold-based methods had 1 TPR and 0 FPR values.
source: At zero noise, both methods had 1 TPR and 0 FPR values (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2a-c showing perfect detection at zero noise.

claim: Increasing noise levels resulted in a parallel decrease in TPR values for both methods.
source: Increasing noise levels resulted in a parallel decrease in TRP values.
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In case of threshold-based method, FPR increased dramatically with increasing noise due to higher fluctuation of pixel values.
source: However, in case of the TBM FPR increased dramatically (cyan dots in Figure 2b) due to the higher fluctuation of pixel values (Figure 2d), which indicates a highly unreliable exclusion of false positive pixels (Figure 2e, circles), while the FPR value in case of Moran's method remained nearly constant (Figure 2e, triangles) with increasing noise.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2b, d, and e showing increased false positives with threshold method.

claim: FPR value in case of Moran's method remained nearly constant with increasing noise.
source: However, in case of the TBM FPR increased dramatically (cyan dots in Figure 2b) due to the higher fluctuation of pixel values (Figure 2d), which indicates a highly unreliable exclusion of false positive pixels (Figure 2e, circles), while the FPR value in case of Moran's method remained nearly constant (Figure 2e, triangles) with increasing noise.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2e showing stable FPR for Moran's method.

claim: In threshold-based method, FPR increase was the consequence of random noise frequently increasing pixel intensity values of the background above the threshold level.
source: In case of TBM FPR increase was the consequence of that random noise frequently increased the pixel intensity values of the background above the threshold level (Figure 2), which were detected as positive pixels.
evidence: This is explained and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: At noise level 80, FPR was significantly lower for Moran's method (0.0085 ± 0.0003) compared to threshold method (0.13333 ± 0.0009), p < 5.4*10^-215.
source: Huge increase in false positive pixels in TBM with increasing noise resulted in significantly lower FPR values compared to that of Moran's (Figure 2e, f, FPR values noise 80: threshold, 0.13333 ± 0.0009, Moran's: 0.0085 ± 0.0003, p < 5.4*10−215; noise 160: threshold, 0.3866 ± 0.0012, Moran, 0.0055 ± 0.0005, p < 2.1*10–244).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e, f.

claim: At noise level 160, FPR was significantly lower for Moran's method (0.0055 ± 0.0005) compared to threshold method (0.3866 ± 0.0012), p < 2.1*10^-244.
source: Huge increase in false positive pixels in TBM with increasing noise resulted in significantly lower FPR values compared to that of Moran's (Figure 2e, f, FPR values noise 80: threshold, 0.13333 ± 0.0009, Moran's: 0.0085 ± 0.0003, p < 5.4*10−215; noise 160: threshold, 0.3866 ± 0.0012, Moran, 0.0055 ± 0.0005, p < 2.1*10–244).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e, f.

claim: At noise level 80, TPR of Moran's method (0.9674 ± 0.0025) was significantly better than threshold method (0.9116 ± 0.0023), p < 2.7*10^-130.
source: TPR of Moran's was also significantly better at noise 80 (Figure 2e, f, TPR values noise 80: threshold, 0.9116 ± 0.0023; Moran's, 0.9674 ± 0.0025, p < 2.7*10–130).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e, f.

claim: At noise level 160, TPR of threshold method (0.6799 ± 0.0041) was marginally better than Moran's method (0.6609 ± 0.0060), p < 5.04*10^-69.
source: The TPR of TBM was marginally better at noise 160 (Figure 2e, f, noise 160: threshold, 0.6799 ± 0.0041; Moran's: 0.6609 ± 0.0060, p < 5.04*10–69), but the difference in FPR values was so large between the two methods that it far outweighed this effect.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e, f.

claim: Quality of detection was significantly better with Moran's method at noise level 80 (FPR/TPR vector: 0.0337 ± 5.8*10^-6) compared to threshold method (0.1600 ± 2.2*10^-6), p < 5*10^-169.
source: Quality of detection was significantly better with Moran's method at both noise levels in a population of 100 randomly generated images (Figure 2e, FPR/TPR vector noise 80: threshold, 0.1600 ± 2.2*10–6; Moran's: 0.0337 ± 5.8*10–6, p < 5*10–169; noise 160: threshold, 0.5019 ± 7.5*10–6, Moran, 0.3391 ± 3.7*10–5, p < 10–156).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Quality of detection was significantly better with Moran's method at noise level 160 (FPR/TPR vector: 0.3391 ± 3.7*10^-5) compared to threshold method (0.5019 ± 7.5*10^-6), p < 10^-156.
source: Quality of detection was significantly better with Moran's method at both noise levels in a population of 100 randomly generated images (Figure 2e, FPR/TPR vector noise 80: threshold, 0.1600 ± 2.2*10–6; Moran's: 0.0337 ± 5.8*10–6, p < 5*10–169; noise 160: threshold, 0.5019 ± 7.5*10–6, Moran, 0.3391 ± 3.7*10–5, p < 10–156).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2e.

claim: With the exception of the lowest noise levels (0-30), Moran's method outperformed threshold-based method at every noise level irrespective of the threshold mostly independent of the exact Moran's order used (range 4-13).
source: We found that with the exception of the lowest noise levels (0–30) Moran's method outperformed TBM at every noise levels irrespective of the threshold mostly independent of the exact Moran's order used (range 4–13; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing systematic comparison across parameters.

claim: Optimal Moran's order was independent of the noise level and was 0.25 times (range: 0.238-0.253) of the object size.
source: We found that optimal Moran's order was independent of the noise level, and it was 0.25 times (range: 0.238–0.253) of the object size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is quantitative data from systematic testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: In threshold-based method at increased noise levels, false positive pixels were homogeneously distributed in the image due to the increased background noise.
source: It is important to emphasize that in the case of TBM at increased noise levels, false positive pixels were homogeneously distributed in the image due to the increased background noise (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3c showing distribution of false positives.

claim: With Moran's method, most false positive pixels surrounded the human-based selection areas.
source: In contrast, with Moran's, most false positive pixels surrounded the human-based selection areas (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3d showing localized false positives.

claim: Moran's method detected out of focus pixels which were routinely not selected by human experts.
source: This is largely the consequence of that Moran's method detected the out of focus pixels as well, which were routinely not selected by the human experts.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with human expert selections.

claim: Voltage-gated ion channels are either distributed homogeneously, along a gradient or form high-density clusters in neuronal membranes.
source: Voltage-gated ion channels are either distributed homogeneously, along a gradient (Lorincz and Nusser, 1979; Kerti et al., 2012) or form high-density clusters in neuronal membranes (Alonso and Widmer, 1997; Kollo et al., 2006; Kollo et al., 2008), endowing neurons with unique electrical properties (Chen et al., 2006; Hoffman et al., 1997; Johnston et al., 2003; Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature on ion channel distribution.

claim: Ion channel distribution patterns endow neurons with unique electrical properties.
source: Voltage-gated ion channels are either distributed homogeneously, along a gradient (Lorincz and Nusser, 1979; Kerti et al., 2012) or form high-density clusters in neuronal membranes (Alonso and Widmer, 1997; Kollo et al., 2006; Kollo et al., 2008), endowing neurons with unique electrical properties (Chen et al., 2006; Hoffman et al., 1997; Johnston et al., 2003; Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on neuronal electrical properties.

claim: The exact subcellular distribution of Kv4.2/4.3 subunits and the logic of their possible clustering in thalamic cells are unknown.
source: However, the exact subcellular distribution of these subunits and the logic of their possible clustering in thalamic cells are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Immunostainings for Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits displayed homogenous, diffuse labeling in the major somatosensory nucleus of the thalamus (VPM).
source: Immunostainings for the Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits displayed homogenous, diffuse labeling in the major somatosensory nucleus of the thalamus (VPM).
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining experiments.

claim: At high magnifications, Kv4 subunits form strongly immunopositive clusters (2-10 µm).
source: At high magnifications, however, it became visually evident that Kv4 subunits also form strongly immunopositive clusters (2–10 µm; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4a showing high magnification images.

claim: Electron microscopic examination confirmed the exclusive dendritic localization of Kv4.2 subunit (n = 123 profiles).
source: To study the precise subcellular distribution of Kv4 subunits, we first examined the Kv4.2 subunit at the electron microscopic level using preembedding immunogold reactions. This approach confirmed the exclusive dendritic localization of this subunit (n = 123 profiles).
evidence: This is data from electron microscopy experiments examining 123 dendritic profiles.

claim: Large caliber dendrites of relay cells displayed a high density of immunogold particles for the Kv4.2 subunit.
source: As suggested by the light microscopic observations, large caliber dendrites of relay cells displayed a high density of immunogold particles for the Kv4.2 subunit (n = 9 animals, Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in electron microscopy images from 9 animals shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: Thick dendrites (minor diameter over 1.2 µm) showed more than three times higher density of Kv4.2 silver particles compared to thin dendrites (minor diameter below 1.2 µm).
source: Quantification of silver particles along the dendritic membranes (n = 3 animals) demonstrated more than three times higher density on thick (minor diameter over 1.2 µm) dendrites, preferentially innervated by large excitatory terminals containing round vesicles (RL terminals) compared to thin (minor diameter below 1.2 µm) dendrites which received very little of this type of inputs (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is quantitative data from 3 animals shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Thick dendrites are preferentially innervated by large excitatory terminals containing round vesicles (RL terminals).
source: Quantification of silver particles along the dendritic membranes (n = 3 animals) demonstrated more than three times higher density on thick (minor diameter over 1.2 µm) dendrites, preferentially innervated by large excitatory terminals containing round vesicles (RL terminals) compared to thin (minor diameter below 1.2 µm) dendrites which received very little of this type of inputs (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Thin dendrites received very little input from large excitatory terminals containing round vesicles.
source: Quantification of silver particles along the dendritic membranes (n = 3 animals) demonstrated more than three times higher density on thick (minor diameter over 1.2 µm) dendrites, preferentially innervated by large excitatory terminals containing round vesicles (RL terminals) compared to thin (minor diameter below 1.2 µm) dendrites which received very little of this type of inputs (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Freeze-fracture replica labeling revealed uneven distribution of gold particles for Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits on large diameter dendrites.
source: Examination of replicas of the VPM immunolabeled for the Kv4.2 or the Kv4.3 subunits revealed gold particles associated with the protoplasmic face of dendritic segments, consistent with the intracellular location of the epitopes. On large diameter dendrites, we observed uneven distribution of gold particles (Figure 4e) consistent with our observations using confocal microscopy and preembedding immunogold localization.
evidence: This is demonstrated in freeze-fracture replica images shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The density of gold particles for Kv4.3 subunit was twice as high in large diameter dendrites (12.6 ± 8.0 gold/µm²) compared to small diameter dendrites (6.0 ± 3.6 gold/µm²).
source: Quantitative evaluation of the reactions in one rat demonstrated that the density of gold particles for the Kv4.3 subunit was twice as high in large, compared to small diameter dendrites (12.6 ± 8.0 gold/µm2, n = 18 vs 6.0 ± 3.6 gold/µm2, n = 18).
evidence: This is quantitative data from freeze-fracture replica labeling in one rat.

claim: The density of gold particles for Kv4.2 subunit was 22.8 ± 8.8 gold/µm² in large diameter proximal dendrites and 9.3 ± 3.2 gold/µm² in small, distal dendrites.
source: A similar difference was found for the Kv4.2 subunit, for which the density of gold particles was 22.8 ± 8.8 gold/µm2 (n = 9) in large diameter proximal dendrites, whereas it was 9.3 ± 3.2 gold/µm2 (n = 6) in small, distal dendrites.
evidence: This is quantitative data from freeze-fracture replica labeling.

claim: Dendritic appendages were decorated with gold particles for Kv4 subunits.
source: Dendritic appendages were also decorated with gold particles (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4h showing gold particles on dendritic appendages.

claim: Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits display weak distal dendritic labeling but proximal, large diameter dendrites contain high densities of these ion channel subunits in VPM.
source: These data together demonstrate that Kv4.2 and Kv4.3 subunits display weak distal dendritic labeling, but the proximal, large diameter dendrites contain high densities of these ion channel subunits in VPM.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the electron microscopy data.

claim: Large, high-density clusters of Kv4.2 ion channels were associated with vGluT2-immunopositive terminals.
source: The data showed that large, high-density clusters of Kv4.2 ion channels were indeed associated with vGluT2-immunopositive terminals (Figure 5e, cyan arrows), whereas the smaller and less intense ones were not (Figure 5f, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated in double immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 5e, f.

claim: Smaller and less intense Kv4.2 clusters were not associated with vGluT2-immunopositive terminals.
source: The data showed that large, high-density clusters of Kv4.2 ion channels were indeed associated with vGluT2-immunopositive terminals (Figure 5e, cyan arrows), whereas the smaller and less intense ones were not (Figure 5f, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated in double immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 5e, f.

claim: Immunopositive Kv4.2 clusters had highly variable sizes (5.59 ± 13.26 µm²) and intensities (745 ± 260 a.u.).
source: Immunopositive clusters generally had highly variable sizes (5.59 ± 13.26 µm2) and intensities (745 ± 260 a.u.).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the segmentation analysis.

claim: The large majority of non-colocalizing Kv4.2 clusters were below 1 µm² and faintly stained.
source: The large majority of the non-colocalizing Kv clusters were below 1 µm2 and faintly stained (Figure 5g) whereas more than the half of the colocalized Kv4.2 structures were above 5 µm2 and more intensely labeled (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the histogram shown in Figure 5g.

claim: More than half of the colocalized Kv4.2 structures were above 5 µm² and more intensely labeled.
source: The large majority of the non-colocalizing Kv clusters were below 1 µm2 and faintly stained (Figure 5g) whereas more than the half of the colocalized Kv4.2 structures were above 5 µm2 and more intensely labeled (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the histogram shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Kv4.2 clusters associated with vGluT2-positive terminals were significantly larger (12.21 ± 18.63 µm²) than Kv4.2 regions outside the vGluT2 terminals (0.90 ± 1.31 µm²).
source: Kv4.2 clusters associated with vGluT2-positive terminals were significantly larger (12.21 ± 18.63 µm2) and more intense (894 ± 280 a.u.) than Kv4.2 regions outside the vGluT2 terminals (average size: 0.90 ± 1.31 µm2, average intensity: 639 ± 182 a.u.) indicating that Moran's I method could delineate functionally relevant ion channel clusters associated with a specific synaptic input (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Kv4.2 clusters associated with vGluT2-positive terminals were more intense (894 ± 280 a.u.) than Kv4.2 regions outside the vGluT2 terminals (639 ± 182 a.u.).
source: Kv4.2 clusters associated with vGluT2-positive terminals were significantly larger (12.21 ± 18.63 µm2) and more intense (894 ± 280 a.u.) than Kv4.2 regions outside the vGluT2 terminals (average size: 0.90 ± 1.31 µm2, average intensity: 639 ± 182 a.u.) indicating that Moran's I method could delineate functionally relevant ion channel clusters associated with a specific synaptic input (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Moran's I method could delineate functionally relevant ion channel clusters associated with a specific synaptic input.
source: Kv4.2 clusters associated with vGluT2-positive terminals were significantly larger (12.21 ± 18.63 µm2) and more intense (894 ± 280 a.u.) than Kv4.2 regions outside the vGluT2 terminals (average size: 0.90 ± 1.31 µm2, average intensity: 639 ± 182 a.u.) indicating that Moran's I method could delineate functionally relevant ion channel clusters associated with a specific synaptic input (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is an inference from the colocalization data shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Membrane segments contacted by vGluT2 boutons showed more than four times higher gold particle density (37.0 particles/100 μm) compared to surrounding membrane surfaces not contacted by vGluT2-positive axons (8.9 particles/100 μm).
source: Membrane segments contacted by vGluT2 boutons showed more than four times higher gold particle density (37.0 particles/100 μm membrane profile, total measured length: 601 μm) compared to surrounding membrane surfaces that were not contacted by vGluT2-positive axons (8.9 particles/100 μm, total measured length: 394 μm).
evidence: This is quantitative data from double immunostaining electron microscopy experiments.

claim: The data reveal a novel association of voltage-gated ion channel clusters on the postsynaptic membrane surfaces with a specialized presynaptic terminal.
source: These data reveal a novel association of voltage-gated ion channel clusters on the postsynaptic membrane surfaces with a specialized presynaptic terminal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined light and electron microscopy data.

claim: Local Moran's method has not been used for image segmentation before this study.
source: Local Moran's method has not been used for image segmentation so far.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the application.

claim: Global Moran's method has been used in a wide range of biomedical image analyses.
source: Its global version, however, has already been utilized in a wide range of biomedical image analyses.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to various applications.

claim: Global Moran's method assigns a value to the whole image and describes whether pixel distribution is random or not, but does not segment pixels to object, no object and noise.
source: Global Moran's method assigns a value to the whole image and describes whether pixel distribution is random or not, but does not segment pixels to object, no object and noise.
evidence: This explains the difference between global and local Moran's methods.

claim: Global Moran's I was used to examine muscle and fat tissue on 3D MRI images.
source: Global Moran's I were used to examine muscle and fat tissue on three-dimensional (3D) MRI (Magnetic Resonant Images) images (Santago et al., 2016) or to measure anisotropy in ultrasound imaging (Ahn and Kaptchuk, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Santago et al., 2016.

claim: Global Moran's method was used to measure anisotropy in ultrasound imaging.
source: Global Moran's I were used to examine muscle and fat tissue on three-dimensional (3D) MRI (Magnetic Resonant Images) images (Santago et al., 2016) or to measure anisotropy in ultrasound imaging (Ahn and Kaptchuk, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahn and Kaptchuk, 2011.

claim: Global Moran's method was used to analyze the homogeneity of temporal information in Ca²⁺ signals in periodontal fibroblasts.
source: In addition, Global Moran's method was also used to analyze the homogeneity of the temporal information in Ca2+ signals in periodontal fibroblasts (Ei Hsu Hlaing et al., 2019) or to detect correlated neuronal activity (Schmal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ei Hsu Hlaing et al., 2019.

claim: Global Moran's method was used to detect correlated neuronal activity.
source: In addition, Global Moran's method was also used to analyze the homogeneity of the temporal information in Ca2+ signals in periodontal fibroblasts (Ei Hsu Hlaing et al., 2019) or to detect correlated neuronal activity (Schmal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmal et al., 2017.

claim: The utilization of Local Moran's method can be extended for 3D image segmentation and analyzing temporal signals.
source: Based on these, the utilization of Local Moran's method, as described here, will not be restricted to segmenting objects on two-dimensional images but can be extended for 3D image segmentation and analyzing temporal signals.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications based on the current work.

claim: The strongest argument to use Local Moran's I instead of threshold-based segmentation is the effective elimination of false positive pixels from the background.
source: The strongest argument to use Local Moran's I instead of threshold-based segmentation is the effective elimination of false positive pixels from the background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative performance data.

claim: White noise does not cause a pattern.
source: Although the intensity of noisy pixels can reach or exceed that of the objects, white noise does not cause a pattern.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of white noise.

claim: Detection of the lack of spatial correlation is a powerful tool to ignore false positive salient pixels in the background.
source: Detection of the lack of spatial correlation is a powerful tool to ignore false positive salient pixels in the background.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism by which Moran's method works.

claim: Selection of the signal with Moran's method is relatively insensitive to the exact matrix size within a certain range (Moran's order 3-8), especially in noisy conditions.
source: We determined that selection of the signal is relatively insensitive of the exact matrix size within a certain range (Moran's order 3–8), especially in noisy conditions.
evidence: This is based on the systematic testing shown in Figure 3f and supplements.

claim: A priori knowledge of the expected object size helps to define the best matrix size.
source: A priori knowledge of the expected object size helps to define the best matrix size since we found a linear correlation between object size and Moran's order for optimal image segmentation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the linear correlation demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a linear correlation between object size and Moran's order for optimal image segmentation.
source: A priori knowledge of the expected object size helps to define the best matrix size since we found a linear correlation between object size and Moran's order for optimal image segmentation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The functional relevance of the association between presynaptic terminal type and postsynaptic ion channel clusters remains to be determined.
source: The functional relevance of this unique association remains to be determined: it may participate in timing the precision of sensory integration, but recently the non-synaptic role of voltage-gated ion channel accumulation has also been proposed (Cserép et al., 2020).
evidence: This acknowledges that the functional significance is not yet established.

claim: The association between presynaptic terminals and ion channel clusters may participate in timing the precision of sensory integration.
source: The functional relevance of this unique association remains to be determined: it may participate in timing the precision of sensory integration, but recently the non-synaptic role of voltage-gated ion channel accumulation has also been proposed (Cserép et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about possible functional roles.

claim: A non-synaptic role of voltage-gated ion channel accumulation has been proposed.
source: The functional relevance of this unique association remains to be determined: it may participate in timing the precision of sensory integration, but recently the non-synaptic role of voltage-gated ion channel accumulation has also been proposed (Cserép et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cserép et al., 2020.

claim: Six adult male C57Bl/6 mice were used to examine Kv4.2 expression.
source: Six adult male C57Bl/6 mice were perfused to examine the Kv4.2 expression.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: VGluT2 is a ubiquitous marker of axon terminals with subcortical origin in the thalamus.
source: These subcortical excitatory inputs were labeled with vesicular glutamate transporter type 2 (vGluT2, Figure 5d; Herzog et al., 2001; Fremeau et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herzog et al., 2001 and Fremeau et al., 2001.

claim: The method normalizes each pixel intensity value as the first step.
source:
In dark field images, contiguous clustered pixels with similarly high intensities represent object (red in Figure 1j), clustered pixels with low intensities indicate no object (e.g., lumen of a blood vessel) (blue in Figure 1j). Group of pixels with random intensity value distribution (which do not reach significance) represent noise (gray in Figure 1j). In bright field images, the picture is reversed, contiguous low- and high-intensity pixels represent the object and no object, respectively (blue and red in Figure 1t).

Local Moran's I differentiates between object, no object, and noise in the following way: the method first normalizes each pixel intensity value (Figure 1c, m) (see Methods).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1c, m.

claim: The method defines a weight matrix in the local neighborhood for each pixel.
source: Next, it defines a weight matrix in the local neighborhood (3 × 3 in this particular case) for each pixel (Figure 1d, n), where the pixel in question receives zero weight.
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1d, n.

claim: The pixel in question receives zero weight in the weight matrix.
source: Next, it defines a weight matrix in the local neighborhood (3 × 3 in this particular case) for each pixel (Figure 1d, n), where the pixel in question receives zero weight.
evidence: This is a specific detail of the method explained in the text and shown in Figure 1d, n.

claim: The method calculates a weighted intensity value for each pixel using the summed values of the neighboring pixels.
source: Then it calculates a weighted intensity value for each pixel in the image using the summed values of the neighboring pixels (Figure 1e, o).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1e, o.

claim: Immediate neighbors of each pixel are assigned with the weight of 1 in first-order matrices.
source: Immediate neighbors of each pixel are assigned with the weight of 1.
evidence: This is a specific detail of the weighting scheme.

claim: The method creates lagged gray values by dividing the matrix values with the number of neighboring pixels.
source: Next, it creates lagged gray values by dividing the matrix values with the number of neighboring pixels (Figure 1f, p).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1f, p.

claim: The method generates the Local Moran's I value for each pixel by multiplying the lagged gray values with the normalized values.
source: Finally, it generates the Local Moran's I value for each pixel by multiplying the lagged gray values (Figure 1f, p) with the normalized values (Figure 1c, m).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The Local Moran's I value represents how the intensity of the pixel and its neighbors differs from the distribution of intensities of all pixels in the image.
source: The resulting Local Moran's I value (Figure 1g, q) will represent how the intensity of the pixel and its neighbors differs from the distribution of intensities of all pixels in the image (clusteredness).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1g, q.

claim: The method determines the probability (pseudosignificance) of obtaining a given Local Moran's I value using Monte Carlo simulations.
source: For each pixel, the method determines the probability (pseudosignificance) of obtaining this or higher Local Moran's I value using Monte Carlo simulations of the intensity values of all pixels in the image (Figure 1h, r).
evidence: This is explained in the methodological description and illustrated in Figure 1h, r.

claim: Significant pixels (p < 0.05) with high intensities in dark field images or low intensities in bright field images are considered as object.
source: Significant pixels (p <0 .05) with high intensities (in case of dark field images) or low intensities (in case of bright filed images) will be considered as object.
evidence: This is the decision rule for classifying pixels as objects.

claim: Consideration of each pixel as signal depends on the combination of spatial arrangement and pixel intensities, not purely on absolute intensity value.
source: As a consequence, in this method consideration of each pixel as signal will not depend purely on the absolute intensity value of the pixel but on the intensity values of the neighboring pixels and the statistical probability that this spatial arrangement can arise (or not) randomly.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the method differs from threshold-based approaches.
